planting.note: Plant grafted or air-layered trees in spring once soil has warmed; in zone 9b–10 plant March–June. Alano is best suited to zones 10–11 but performs in protected zone 9b microclimates where winter lows rarely drop below 28°F. Young trees need frost protection their first two winters; established trees tolerate brief dips into the upper 20s°F with only leaf damage. Fruiting is year-round once mature, with the heaviest flush in late spring through summer.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor, alkaline-tolerant soil — Alano is one of the few high-quality sapodilla cultivars that sets fruit reliably on South Florida's rocky, calcareous soils. The round to oval fruits have smooth, thin skin and fine-grained, low-grit tan flesh with a rich, malty, brown-sugar sweetness that Florida growers rank among the best-flavored sapodilla selections available, distinct from and often preferred over 'Brown Sugar' for its smoother texture. Trees are self-fertile, wind-tolerant, and extremely drought-hardy once established, needing supplemental water mainly during establishment and dry fruit-set periods. Harvest fruit when it develops a dull, scurfy skin and yields slightly to gentle pressure, then ripen off the tree for several days at room temperature before eating.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sapodilla Cultivars for Florida
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Sapodilla Variety Trials
California Rare Fruit Growers — Sapodilla Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant air-layered or grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Diamond River is noted among longan cultivars for superior cold hardiness, with mature wood surviving brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s°F that would kill standard longan cultivars to the ground — this makes it the preferred selection for Central and North Florida and coastal zone 9 Gulf plantings. Like other longans it benefits from a brief cool, dry winter rest to trigger flowering, which occurs naturally in zone 9.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Diamond River is a Florida-selected longan valued for combining good fruit quality with markedly better cold tolerance than 'Kohala' and other tropical longan selections, allowing it to be grown successfully in zone 9 areas of the Gulf South where longan was historically considered too tender to fruit reliably. Clusters of thin-shelled, tan-brown fruit ripen in mid-to-late summer, with sweet, juicy, translucent flesh similar in flavor to lychee but more floral and less acidic. Prune young trees to an open, low-branched form for wind resistance and ease of frost-cloth coverage during establishment; mature trees need protection only in unusually severe freezes.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Longan Growing in the Home Landscape
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Longan and Lychee for Gulf South
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Cold-Hardy Longan Selections for South Texas

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Vernon is among the more cold-tolerant white sapote cultivars, with mature trees withstanding brief lows in the mid-20s°F with only minor twig damage, making it a workable choice for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree will set fruit without a pollinator. Fruit ripens over an extended window from fall into winter depending on climate.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil sheltered from strong wind; Vernon is a California-bred white sapote selection prized for consistent, heavy production and self-fertility, removing the need to plant a second tree for pollination as some white sapote cultivars require. The medium-sized, thin-skinned, green-to-yellow fruit has smooth, custard-textured flesh with a sweet flavor often compared to a blend of banana, peach, and vanilla pudding. Trees grow fast and can reach substantial size, so plan for eventual shade and root spread; prune after harvest to maintain a manageable height and encourage branching for next season's crop. Fruit is ready to pick when it softens slightly and yields to gentle pressure, then finishes ripening at room temperature over several days.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Subtropical Fruit Trees for South Texas

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 9b–10 plant March–June. Maher is best suited to zones 10–11, though it can succeed in warm, protected zone 9b microclimates near the coast. Young trees need frost protection; established trees tolerate brief dips to near 27°F but suffer significant dieback below that. Fruit ripens in fall and early winter, later than most other Gulf Coast tree fruits.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Maher is a Florida-selected black sapote valued for its large, round, apple-green fruit that ripens to a dull olive-brown and reveals dark, chocolate-brown, custard-smooth flesh once fully soft — hence the common name 'chocolate pudding fruit.' Unlike astringent persimmons, black sapote is only palatable when completely soft-ripe, at which point the mild, sweet flesh is eaten fresh with a spoon or blended into puddings, smoothies, and baked goods. Trees are attractive, glossy-leaved evergreens that tolerate light shade better than most fruit trees, making them useful in mixed edible plantings. Harvest fruit while still firm and green and allow it to fully soften indoors over one to two weeks, as tree-ripened fruit is quickly taken by wildlife.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Black Sapote in the Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Black Sapote Variety Notes
California Rare Fruit Growers — Black Sapote Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; in zone 10 plant March–June. Mamey sapote is a true tropical suited to zones 10–11 and is not reliable in zone 9; young trees are damaged by any frost and mature trees are injured below about 29°F. Give it the warmest, most wind-sheltered spot available in coastal South Florida or South Texas plantings. Pantin fruits mainly in summer, with fruit taking well over a year to mature from flower to harvest.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil with room for a large canopy; Pantin is one of the oldest and most widely planted named mamey sapote cultivars in South Florida, tracing to early Cuban plantings in Miami-Dade County, and remains a benchmark for commercial-quality fruit. The large, football-shaped fruit has rough, russet-brown skin and dense, salmon-pink to brick-red flesh with a rich, sweet flavor often described as a cross between pumpkin, sweet potato, and almond. Trees are vigorous, long-lived, and eventually very large, so site them well away from structures and power lines. Harvest by scratching the skin lightly — ready fruit shows green beneath the russet surface — then ripen at room temperature for several days to a week until it yields to gentle pressure.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mamey Sapote Growing in Florida
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mamey Sapote Cultivar History
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tropical Fruit Trees for the Rio Grande Valley

planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling-grown trees in spring; in zone 9b–10 plant March–May. Canistel is more cold-tolerant than most egg-fruit relatives, with established Fairchild trees recovering from brief dips into the upper 20s°F. Young trees need frost protection for their first two winters. Fruit ripens over a long season from late summer into winter.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to sandy soil; Fairchild is a long-established Florida canistel selection known for smooth-textured, deep golden-orange flesh with the dense, dry, custard-like texture that gives the fruit its common name, 'egg fruit.' The flavor is sweet and mealy, often likened to a baked sweet potato or boiled egg yolk sweetened with brown sugar, and the flesh is popular blended into shakes, flans, and baked desserts throughout South Florida and the Caribbean. Trees are attractive, glossy-leaved evergreens that tolerate a range of soils and are relatively wind-firm. Pick fruit when the skin turns fully glossy orange-yellow and let it finish softening at room temperature for several days before eating, as canistel is only palatable when fully ripe and soft.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Canistel Growing in the Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Canistel and Related Pouteria Species
California Rare Fruit Growers — Canistel Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted plants in spring after frost danger passes; in zone 9 plant March–May. B-17 acerola is a fast-fruiting shrub that can flower and set fruit within its first year under warm conditions. Established plants tolerate light frost and resprout from the base after a hard freeze, but repeated hard freezes will prevent fruiting. Plants flower and fruit in flushes throughout the warm season, roughly every six to eight weeks.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; B-17 is a selected acerola cultivar developed in Puerto Rico for larger fruit size and heavier yields than seedling acerola, while retaining the species' famously high vitamin C content, among the highest of any fruit. The small, bright-red, cherry-like fruits are thin-skinned, juicy, and tart, best used fresh in juice, syrups, and preserves rather than fresh eating alone since the flavor is quite acidic. The dense, rounded shrub can be maintained as a hedge or specimen and bears repeatedly through the warm months, making it one of the most productive fruiting shrubs for Gulf Coast home gardens. Fruit is highly perishable once ripe and should be harvested promptly and processed or refrigerated within a day or two.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Acerola Growing in the Home Landscape
University of Puerto Rico Agricultural Experiment Station — Acerola Cultivar Development
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Barbados Cherry for South Texas Gardens
